CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION DECISION SOUGHT ON GANANOQUE CABLE TELEVISION LICENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring the attention of this House to the continuing saga of the Town of Gananoque and its seven-year battle with CRTC to obtain cable television service. This town is located in the Toronto-Montreal corridor, and it is amazing in today's technologically advanced society that Gananoque is still in the stone age.
Seven years ago a licence to provide cable service was approved by CRTC but the company had difficulty in fulfilling the requirements, and CRTC was forced to lift the licence from the company. Last September CRTC received two submissions to provide cable service to Gananoque. Eight months have passed with no decision forthcoming, despite my repeated communications with the Chairman, and his assurances that it was a high priority item.
No response to my representations can only lead me to conclude that the Government cares little for the needs of a small community which cannot compete with the mandarins in their ivory towers. It is unthinkable that a government Department given a mandate to provide service to the public is so insensitive that it refuses to cut through its own bureaucratic red tape and produce a decision on whether company A or company B should be licensed.
It is long past the time when Gananoque should have had cable service, and I call upon the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) to intervene on its behalf to obtain a decision immediately, ending a seven-year long battle to obtain what most communities in this country have, cable vision service.

NATIONAL REVENUE
subsubtopic: TAX TREATMENT OF WORKERS' HOLIDAY PAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the end of this month workers at the Gardiner Denver plant in Woodstock, Ontario, will be laid off because the plant is closing its doors. All of the workers have earned holiday pay for the amount of time they were employed by the plant. The Revenue Canada District Office in London, Ontario, has instructed the payroll clerk at the plant to consider holiday pay as bonus pay and to withhold 40 per cent of the employee's final cheques. Revenue Canada claims that when workers take holiday pay instead of holidays, they are attempting to increase their annual salary, and the 40 per cent deduction is there to discourage this practice.
There is, however, another provision of the Employer's Guide issued by Revenue Canada which allows a 15 per cent tax withholding. This is more in line with the standard payroll deductions for these workers. If the 15 per cent figure were used instead of 40 per cent, it could mean an increase of between $600 and $2,000 immediate cash for the workers at this plant who are about to be laid off with little prospect of further employment. Revenue Canada is penalizing laid-off workers by using a provision in the Guide designed in times of greater employment, and which today is simply and needlessly taking money out of people's pockets. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) should immediately instruct his Department to apply the 15 per cent standard deduction instead of the 40 per cent penalty.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am on my feet again to address the problems in the tobacco and related industries. A 32 per cent cut in tobacco production is proposed for this year. That will relate directly to 800 farms not in production, a loss of some 10,000 jobs, and a $100
million loss to growers. Using an economic factor of six, that means a $600 million loss to local communities and businesses.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: WOMAN'S FAST TO SECURE REUNIFICATION OF FAMILY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today is the twenty-third day without food for Kazimiera Cebula, a courageous 50 year old woman who asks nothing more than to be reunited with her son, Janusz Lata, and his wife and children. She has been outside the Polish consulate in Montreal in rain and snow, with her companion, Ewa Szypura, who has learned that her husband and daughter will receive exist visas from Poland, but who has chosen to continue her 19 day old fast out of solidarity with her compatriot. They are dangerously weak, but determined to see their families.
Since the hunger strikes of other desperate people at Polish consulates, both in Montreal and Toronto last year, all of which were ended without tragedy, the Polish Government continues to violate the most basic of human rights, the reunification of families, guaranteed in the Helsinki Accord to which Poland is a signatory. With calculated inhumanity, some Polish citizens, often former members of the trade union Solidarity, continue to be blackmailed into leaving their homeland, while others are held to ransom and denied exit visas.
I wish to extend my deep felt sympathy and encouragement to these two brave women and to the many families suffering a similar plight. I urge the Department of External Affairs, which I understand has issued visas for all the persons concerned, to strengthen its representations to the Polish Government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a brief question of privilege relating to the use of parliamentary facilities and privileges for non-parliamentary purposes.
As you may recall, Mr. Speaker, in response to a question of privilege raised by the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) in February of 1978, Mr. Speaker Jerome outlined a set of general guidelines for a policy on the use of the Parliament Buildings. At that time, the Hon. Member voiced his concern about the fact that the Liberal Party was intending to make use of parliamentary facilities in conjunction with a Liberal Party convention which was being held in Ottawa.
Mr. Speaker Jerome observed:
Anything taking place in these buildings certainly ought to have a parliamentary connection and ought to be in keeping with a number of conditions that respect the dignity of the premises.
His full comments may be found in the Debates for February 14, 1978, at pages 2833 and 2834.
I happened to walk past the post office entrance to the Centre Block on my way into the building this morning. As you will know, Mr. Speaker, a variety of general information is left on tables and notice boards in and around the foyer at the post office entrance. This information usually relates to job vacancies and competitions, charitable appeals and other information of general interest to employees of the House of Commons or to Members' employees. You can no doubt imagine therefore, Mr. Speaker, how surprised I was to discov-
April 18, 1984

er that, along with all of the other notices and literature, were three cartons of pamphlets extolling the virtues of a certain John Turner and bearing the logo of the Liberal Party of Canada.
The pamphlets were issued in the name of an organization called "The Friends of John Turner" and take the form of an open letter "To Liberals in Canada" from the Hon. Member for Terrebonne (Mr. Comtois) and a Franqoise Gagnon. The letter solicits support for Mr. Turner and asks that the attached form be filled in and returned "quickly" by those who agree with "The Friends of John Turner". The form, in part, reads as follows:
I support wholeheartedly the movement to favour the election of JOHN TURNER as Leader of the Liberal Party of Canada and Prime Minister of Canada and I want to join his team.
Mr. Speaker, I have no doubt that "The Friends of John Turner", the Hon. Member for Terrebonne included, have nothing but the highest of motives in mind in causing this pamphlet to be printed and distributed. I am certain that Mr. Turner, whoever he may be, needs all the friends he can get as "quickly" as possible. Nonetheless, I question whether leaving these pamphlets out for distribution in the post office entrance to the Centre Block is an activity which has a parliamentary connection or which respects the dignity of the premises as outlined by Mr. Speaker Jerome. I might add, Mr. Speaker, that when last I checked, the cartons and material in question had been removed, 1 understand by the Sergeant-at-Arms. However, Mr. Speaker, if such activities continue to occur I see nothing which would prevent the other leadership candidates from setting up tables in various places around the building to sell memberships in the Liberal Party or pass out buttons and balloons.
According to press reports, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Terrebonne left these pamphlets in the place that he did because certain translation errors had been made and because he wished to have the pamphlets destroyed. He is further reported to have said that new literature is being prepared and that he intends to distribute these pamphlets by making use of his franking privileges as a Member of Parliament.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jacques Olivier (Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)):

subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
1. The Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) did not offer to take athletes who did not meet the Olympic selection criteria to the 1984 Olympics as guests of the Government.
The Minister did extend an invitation to athletes in the sports of Nordic Combined and Biathlon to observe the Games (as guests of the federal Government), after the Canadian Olympic Association declined to select any athletes to represent Canada in these sports at the Sarajevo Olympics.
There are no minimum criteria for selection for the Olympics in these two sports laid down by either the International Olympic Committee or the International Federations which control the two sports.
With respect to criteria for the Olympics being set two years prior to the Games, the criteria referred to are, presumably, the general selection principles set out by the Canadian Olympic Association-not by the Canadian sport governing bodies responsible for these two sports in Canada.
Further, while the general selection principles were set out by the Canadian Olympic Association in mid-1982 subsequent discussions between the COA and officials of Sport Canada led to an agreement to select athletes who were 1988 potential athletes provided that the federal Government paid for these athletes, and provided that these athletes were clearly participants in long-range training programs aimed at 1988. In the final analysis, when the actual selections were announced in January 1984, these athletes who will likely represent Canada in Calgary in 1988 were denied the Olympic experience in 1984, and so the Minister offered to send them to Sarajevo as observers.
With respect to the process of setting criteria, since Canada became the host nation for 1988 only in mid-1982 and made a major financial commitment to preparing athletes for 1988 in early 1983 (including a doubling of resources to $50 million
for the period from 1983-88), it appears reasonable that the approach of Canada's host nation status and major financial commitments to success in 1988. This answers the question of whether sport organizations' budgets were set based on meeting criteria for selection to the Games. Clearly other factors intervened after the initial criteria had been set-but in any event, budgetary factors were not an issue.
2. No, the Government will not generally intervene in the administration of national sport governing bodies. But, yes, the Government will attempt to prevail on the judgment of organizations such as the Canadian Olympic Association to establish selection standards which will assist in the fulfillment of a public interest in Canada's eventual success in international sport as evidenced by an annual federal Government expenditure on sport of nearly $50 million.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration from April 17, 1984 of the motion of Mr. MacEachen that Bill C-32, an Act to establish the Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence.

subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The last speaker was the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro). There are five minutes remaining in the questions and answer period. Is the Hon. Member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko) rising to put a question? The Hon. Member for Edmonton East on debate.
International Peace and Security

subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the culmination of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) peace initiative we have before us Bill C-32, an Act to establish the Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security. The principles involved in this legislation are sound. Let us cease this ongoing nitpicking and send this legislation to committee where we can adjust the language and change "shalls" to "mays" if advisable. Let us get on with this legislation. With regard to the principles behind this legislation, we need only ask whether it is needed, what its dimensions are to be, and where the institute shall be located.
Let us first ask ourselves whether peace is possible in our world today or if it is a social illusion. When the differences in affluence and poverty are so great between world segments, and when ideologies are a major conflict as to the very purpose of life itself, can lasting peace be a reality? What universal intelligence or universal spirituality can decree that humanity is not bent on self-destruction? What are the characteristics of peace and how are they to be taught and promoted? Can we aim so high as to state that through trust we shall promote international brotherhood and goodwill and through understanding we shall be free from oppression of body and spirit and from uncertainty and fear? Can we state that to understand we must study and analyse and to trust we must discern and know?
We must establish the mechanism to analyse and to understand and then to know and to trust so that we might live without fear, apprehension and oppression. To know and to understand we need a centre of study and analysis and projection and dissemination of information on arms control and defence. Yes, Mr. Speaker, the need is there. The need for an institute for international peace and security is timely.
Where should this institute be located, Mr. Speaker? Let me again suggest that it should be located in Edmonton, halfway between Washington and Moscow, midway between our two mighty neighbours that are armed to the teeth with nuclear weapons.
When we officially open the institute let us invite the President of the United States and the Chairman and President of the U.S.S.R. to cut the ribbon and then to shake hands and have their summit meeting. Every second year these two giants of peace or war should be invited to revisit the institute in Edmonton. Let us bring together in this peace institute in Edmonton both American and Russian experts so that they might learn to communicate, because knowledge and communication should be the prime objectives of this institute.
When I spoke in the Throne Speech debate on January 24 this year, I said:
Some international superpower agreements on the military use of space must be realized in the next five years. Initially, the nuclear delivery mechanisms involved hours in their delivery time.. . This has now been reduced to minutes... and space deployment will reduce the time frame for delivery to seconds.
War by accident and massive escalation will then be beyond the control and reason of man and totally under the control of computers. To the modern mind,

April 18, 1984
International Peace and Security
technological development is the very essence of mankind. Without technological progress some people believe we die as a human race. The very pride of man decrees that space will be conquered and space systems both for military and peaceful use will be developed and deployed. That is the general view in America today.
I suspect it is the general view in Russia.
What we must find is the human will to rationalize and then regulate these systems for the continued constructive evolution of civilization itself. The converse is only darkness.
The institute must study all aspects of accidental initiation of nuclear war. It must develop systems to provide instant communications between the two superpowers to prevent and halt massive escalation.
Indeed, I have frequently envisaged a communications satellite positioned in a stationary orbit above the North Pole which would provide instant communications between the U.S.A. and Russian military commanders and heads of states in order to prevent accidental war and massive escalation.
Surely a Canadian institute for peace would at least perform such a function. Surely one of its first tasks would be to examine the possibilities and the probabilities of launching such a communication satellite. Indeed, the Canadian Government should undertake discussions immediately with both the United States and the Russian Governments to initiate such a satellite project.
Without much more fuss, let us pass this legislation on principle and send it to committee for some minor refinements. Let us give it third reading and get on with the establishment of the institute in Edmonton. Edmonton is the place. Let us get it away from Ottawa, the political centre of Canada, so that political interference in its functions can be minimal.
If we locate it in Edmonton, I feel quite certain that within a few years, or even a few months, it would be named the Pierre Trudeau Institute for International Peace and Security. It would be a fitting tribute to a Prime Minister who really tried to do his best for world peace and now rides into the sunset.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to the use of weapons in space, let me say first that I am of the opinion that technological progress in regard to the use of space both for military and peaceful purposes cannot be stopped. It will go ahead irrespective of what is said in this Parliament or in almost any congress or parliament. I have tended to touch on that matter in several speeches I have made in the House. The question in my mind is the deployment of the deadly device
April 18, 1984

itself, the nuclear weapon. There are now 50,000 in the world. We have to return to the question of reducing the number.
The danger is not with the development of technology because all technology that is developed, whether it is the jeep or the initial airplane, can be used for destruction or construction. Indeed, we have gone through several systems in which the initial development was for military purposes but then they have been used massively for commercial or peaceful purposes.
I cannot think of any single development in technology that has not gone through this variation from possible military use to usefulness in society. I suggest that we must deal with reducing the number of nuclear bombs themselves.
One of the most interesting aspects, of course, is Canada's position in regard to the CANDU nuclear reactor. Canada is trying to market nuclear reactors all over the world in a very significant fashion. I know quite a bit about CANDU reactors because I have worked on the design of some. Yet this is a reactor that we sell which makes it possible to build a nuclear bomb without too much difficulty. We must examine closely our position in regard to the development of technology. I am not suggesting that we should not sell CANDU reactors. That is my answer to the first question.
With respect to the second question regarding the testing of nuclear Cruise missiles, I have stated my position in the House very emphatically. I think I was the first person in the House to take a position in respect of testing the Cruise missile. It was that we should go ahead. To support that view, I return to the process of verifiability and the timeframe for delivery systems. The Cruise missile is a slow delivery system. I feel rather safe with the Cruise missile, as I feel with an airplane, because I believe that nuclear war can start by design, which is first strike capability, if you wish; by escalation as a result of initiation by a small country, such as one in the Middle East; or by accident. I do not fear the first alternative at all. I know of no nation that will start a nuclear war knowing that it will accelerate very rapidly and will not stop until the world is destroyed.
I fear the second instance, of a bomb dropped in Israel, the Middle East, or somewhere else, which act of aggression would then escalate. But I mostly fear the third alternative. I am a technologist. I have worked on nuclear reactors and I know how accidents can happen. My fear is that the Cruise missile has a slow delivery. We have time to react. It is verifiable-not the Cruise missile itself but the bomb itself when it is stationed at some particular point. The bomb is verifiable. A nuclear bomb when it is stationed somewhere brings around it a massive system of protection against somebody stealing it. There is no harm in stealing a Cruise missile. The harm is in stealing the bomb. It is the bomb that will provide the verifiability with respect to the protection systems around it. With respect to the Cruise missile, it is slow. It will give us time to react and stop any escalation process. Second, the nuclear bomb itself and its location is a verifiable process.

subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I was saying, I subscribe fully to the sentiments of the Secretary of State for External Affairs in the expressions that he made and to the Government's commitment to search for world peace and security. Today's strategic environment is characterized, as you well know, Mr. Speaker, by uncertainty and by change. It is essential, therefore, that we all understand the nature of the world in which we live so that we might effectively provide for our security and that of all peoples.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) embarked on his initiative with the intention of defusing some of the worrying aspects of the East-West relations and seeking a way out of the current preoccupation with military strength. He strove to give new political impetus to the search for accommodation. The institute is being proposed in this spirit.
As Minister of National Defence, I support every effort to strengthen peace. My Department and myself are devoting time and effort to work with other Departments, especially the Department of External Affairs, in looking for ways to achieve arms control and disarmament. I am pleased to say that all these initiatives, the latest of which is the proposed Canadian Institute of International Peace and Security, will complement the work of my Department, of which I have the honour to be Minister.
Our defence policies have long been aimed at preserving peace and security and need no elaboration here. One only has to look at the experience of Canada in peace-keeping operations. We have used our military forces, not to make war but to secure peace. We have been the greatest contributor to the United Nations peace-keeping operations, having participated in each one of the peace-keeping operations mounted by that international institute.
As the Secretary of State for External Affairs has said, Canada's investment in defensive collective security agreements has been consistent since the Second World War and has paid the dividend of peace for more than a generation of Canadians. Again, as Minister of National Defence, I support whole-heartedly the act to establish the Canadian institute. The institute, by adding to our store of public knowledge and understanding of the issues has a real contribution to make to the preservation of peace and security. The Department of National Defence will demonstrate its commitment by financing 50 per cent of the institute's budget in partnership with the Department of External Affairs.
Although some of those who are newly aware of the question of peace and security and strategic studies may tend to feel that there is an instant solution somewhere if only goodwill
could be found, we recognize that the issue is an eminently complex one and needs to have a great deal of attention and concentration given to it if we are to make any progress.
The Members of this House are aware of the activities of the Department of National Defence and know that for many years, the Department has played a continuing and active role in the field of research on peace and security. A large part of these activities are carried out by the Operational Research and Analysis Establishment, which works together with the policy planning staff of the Department of National Defence.
The subject is a very important one, Mr. Speaker, and the group in question carries out studies that are to be used in formulating departmental policy, more particularly in the field of East-West relations. In many cases, it has also provided assistance to the Department of External Affairs, when so requested, in the field of analysis. Projects were either short or long-term, and some might be classified while others would be for public release. Often, outside help has been obtained, and research projects on a variety of subjects connected with Canada's defence have been entrusted to eminent academics. In recent years, research on, and analysis of, problems relating to arms control and disarmament has been stressed, with special emphasis on areas where Canada plays an active role, such as reduction in conventional forces and the development of confidence and security in Europe.
In addition, the Operational Research and Analysis Establishment has concentrated on the repercussions that a balance of nuclear power and increasing use of space for military purposes might have for Canada.
Since the foregoing has been the subject of various studies within my Department, the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was able to call on the Department's expertise to help establish strategy for his peace initiative. Similarly, my Department has extended its activities beyond its own confines by encouraging and supporting civilian universities as part of the Military and Strategic Studies Program. Started in 1967, the program's major objective has been to encourage the training of Canadian experts on military and strategic issues, in order to respond to present and future security requirements and arouse a nationwide interest in these issues.
Mr. Speaker, it is common knowledge that the program had humble beginnings. In fact, at the outset, interest in the program was not universal. However, it now helps support five research centres located at the University of British Columbia, the University of Calgary, Queen's University, Laval University and Dalhousie University, and also three teaching centres which are located at York University, the University of New Brunswick and Acadia University. The program also provides a number of bursaries for Canadian university students desiring to pursue a course of study in areas related to national
April 18, 1984

security. The administration of the program is strictly neutral, and the Department does not try to influence the universities. The Military and Strategic Studies Program has been remarkably successful, considering its relatively low budget. I may add that this week, representatives of participating universities, with senior officials responsible for the program, will be meeting in Ottawa at their annual convention.

I have described briefly to the House how the Department uses and promotes the research function associated with national security both within and outside the Department. These DND programs are tailored to the broad needs of national security and will continue to do so. At the same time we must recognize recent developments which led the Government to consider the formation of the Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security as necessary, desirable and complementary to the work of others in the field of military and strategic studies.
The first of these developments is the explosion of information in the field of military and strategic studies. The Speech from the Throne referred to the need for a publicly-funded centre to gather, collate and digest the enormous volume of information now available on defence and arms control issues. As Minister I can attest to the volume and I can see how difficult it is even for trained personnel to understand and assimilate the flow of information. I tend to be on a large number of mailing lists these days. I tend to receive a large volume of documents from a large number of sources. I am not belittling the information which is being provided nor the opinions which are being advanced, because more thought is being given to the particular issue of peace and security than to any other issue facing public administrators and individuals concerned with the public interest.
There is a clear need to collate, collect and digest information and a responsibility to communicate. We as Members of Parliament, men in public life, recognize the need for communications. We recognize how difficult communications are, especially when the issues are so complex and imbued with emotionalism.
The second development is the increase in public interest in matters of peace and security. I can vouch for the fact that since I assumed this particular responsibility public interest in the issue is much greater. I can well understand why. One has only to look at the developments and the difficulties in 1983. Of course, 1983 was the period when the western alliance had to implement its two-track policy with the beginning of the deployment of modernized delivery systems in western Europe. It was the time of the Korean airlines flight No. 007 being shot down and of an increase in tension. Indeed there was and is an ongoing concern. Historically Canadians have tended to be relatively disinterested in peacetime-and I stress in peacetime-in matters of peace and security because Canada has had the major advantage of having seas which isolate it from major threats. Also, we have a very friendly neighbour-and we are very lucky in that respect-on our southern border. Relatively speaking, Canadians have felt very secure. Indeed,
International Peace and Security there was a period of time when the interest relating to these issues was not that great. However, now there are clear signs that the public is no longer content to leave these issues only to professionals and even to politicians. There is a genuine desire to learn more about the complex issues of peace and security.
Ten years ago it was difficult to attract students to military and strategic studies programs. Today there are 598 undergraduates taking military and strategic studies at three teaching centres, and many more than could be accepted within the limits of the current graduate program. At the graduate level, four times as many students applied for scholarships than could be accepted within the funds available. The establishment of the proposed institute will greatly facilitate response to this increased public interest.
One of the characteristics of both the increased public awareness and the explosion of information is the wide variety of opinions expressed. No single Department of government could hope to encompass this spectrum of concerned public opinion, least of all the Department of National Defence because its attention, of necessity, must focus upon giving effect to the Government's security and defence policies. It is the Canadian democratic tradition to seek consensus and reconciliation, not to polarize the discussion of peace and security into what the Secretary of State for External Affairs has called a dialogue of the deaf.
We reaffirm our determination to maintain a strong defence in co-operation with our democratic allies. At the same time we must recognize the overriding imperative to explore new ideas which will go beyond the historic and traditional concepts of national and international security.
There is going to be, of course, a by-product. As the institute gets involved in areas of public concern and in communicating views relating to various solutions and the various positions being proposed, that will make Canadians more conscious of the fact that they belong to a global community. In the past, we have tended to be rather insular. During Question Period very seldom are questions asked relating to international concerns and to peace and security issues. It is to be hoped that with this institute, the internationalization of our interest will be secured and Canadians will become more and more aware of the great world out there and the fact that decisions made outside of Ottawa and the provincial capitals have an impact on their day to day lives.

One has the opportunity to read carefully speeches and comments made by other Members on the previous day of debate. I did that this morning as I was unable to be in the House yesterday morning because of other commitments. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark). Yesterday afternoon when I was present in the House, I listened to the comments made by the Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) and the Hon. Member for Don Valley West (Mr. Bosley) and agreed completely with much of what they had to say.
I think it is clear that for the most part, all Members of the House of Commons are in support of the general intention of this Bill. However, I believe that there is no doubt that all Members and particularly those of us on this side of the House, have some problems with some of the proposals contained in the Bill.
Last December, we heard a Throne Speech that was rather bland and without much promise but that contained a couple of paragraphs which gave us some hope. I will quote the

-the Government will create a publicly funded centre to gather, collate and digest the enormous volume of information now available on defence and arms control issues. Fresh ideas and new proposals, regardless of source, will be studied and promoted.
At the time, Mr. Speaker, many of us in the House considered that portion of the Throne Speech as being a victory of sorts. As my colleague, the Hon. Member for New Westmin-ster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett), said yesterday, we in this Party have always been in favour, remain in favour and will continue to be in favour, of the establishment of some sort of Canadian peace research institute.
It was another sort of victory for me because two years ago this month, I was a member of a group of parliamentarians which included Members from all three Parties, which put out what was known at that time as "Security and Disarmament: A Minority Report." At that time, we called upon the Canadian Government to accept the proposal made by former Secretary General of the United Nations Waldheim that governments contribute one-tenth of 1 per cent of their defence budgets toward disarmament and peace efforts. We specifically recommended that Canada use such money to strengthen disarmament education, information and research activities. We recommended particularly that the Department of External Affairs establish chairs on disarmament or peace research studies at Canadian universities in an attempt to counterbalance the chairs on strategic studies which are funded by the Department of National Defence.
While the efforts the Government is making at the present time as indicated by this Bill do not yet approach an expenditure of one-tenth of 1 per cent of the defence budget, we welcome these efforts as being a positive step toward achieving the Waldheim formula When the Government tabled this Bill the other day, I was pleased to learn that the Government would actually live up to one of the promises made in the Throne Speech.
That does not always happen. I do not think any of us in the House will deny the fact that over the last few years, there has been a dramatic growth of concern among Canadians about the possibilities of a nuclear war. There have been fears expressed about the too rapidly escalating arms race. At the same time as the concerns of Canadians have grown, many Canadians have questioned whether or not the Canadian Government is doing all that is possible and all that is within its powers to alleviate international tensions and to turn around the arms race.
While we welcomed to a certain degree the initiatives taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) last fall, we were as well critical of some of the contradictions in those initiatives. We questioned whether or not the Government has done as much as it could. This afternoon, I do not want to concentrate on the specifics of the concerns of Canadians about a possible nuclear war. I do not want to talk of my fears or of the fears of Canadians in that regard. I do not want to talk about the horrors of a nuclear war, nor do I want to talk about issues in

Central America, the Cruise missile or Canada's involvement in the development and construction of nuclear weapon components. 1 think I have spoken often enough both in and out of the House about those issues. As well, that is really not the point we are debating here today.
When I learned of the introduction of this Bill, I had two hopes for what would be contained in the Bill. I would have thought that what I had hoped for is rather obvious. First, I hoped that the mandate of the institute would be to concentrate on the studies of issues of peace and disarmament. Second, I hoped that the institute would enjoy enough independence from government to gain universal credibility and to be able to criticize existing government policy if it sought to do so.
It has been said in debate during the last day and a half that for too long we as Canadians have had to rely on offshore information and analyses. Canadians who are interested in the subject have not had available to them a large amount of information and analyses that deal with the issues from a strictly Canadian perspective. As my colleague, the Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam, said yesterday, we have in a sense lost some of our independence because we have not had access to information within Canada.
Many Canadians and Members of the House feel that the Canadian institute on peace research studies should follow the example of SIPRI, the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. As has been pointed out by Members on all sides of the House, SIPRI has gained a high degree of credibility, stature and respect throught the world community. It is the Institute which many of us think the Canadian Government should use as an example when setting up the Canadian institute.
One of the things that is most striking about the Stockholm Institute is that it is completely independent of Government. It is funded by the Swedish Parliament, but the Government keeps its hand off the Institute. The Government does not get involved with the Institute by indicating which studies it wants the Institute to undertake. I would say, Mr. Speaker, that if the Canadian Government intends to keep some kind of a hands-on control of the Canadian institute, and if it is not prepared to allow it complete independence from Parliament, from Cabinet, and from possible political interference, then I would say that the Government is simply wasting both public money and the time of this House in setting it up. I would think that under those kinds of circumstances it will not enjoy the credibility it requires to make a meaningful contribution to Canada's public search for peace and disarmament.
There are probably three areas which I have been able to find in this Bill which make me suspect that it is not going to be as independent as we would like to see it. First of all, despite the assertion that the institute will not be an agency of the Crown, Cabinet will still have the power to order the board of directors to repeal, amend or make whatever new by-laws the Government requires or desires. Second, the Government
will be able to influence what topics are examined by the institute. That is because one of the purposes of the institute is to foster, fund and conduct research of particular interest to the Government of Canada. Third, the institute, under Clause 28-which was debated at great length yesterday in this House-shall be required to research for or provide advice on the peace and security issues with which the Minister wants to deal.
I am not quite sure why the Government wants to do this, Mr. Speaker. First of all, it is not lacking in other agencies which have the power and capability of researching issues of special interest to the Government. In the Department of External Affairs there is a committee of deputy ministers. There is also the arms control and disarmament division. In the Department of National Defence there is a director general of strategic policy. There is an office of the director of nuclear arms control policy. The operational research establishment has its own director for strategic analysis. The defence research establishment conducts research into issues of nuclear, biological, chemical warfare, and so on. There are in place a number of government agencies which have the power to give the Government the capability to study issues of its own interest. Why does it want to tie the hands of this new institute we are setting up today?
I would agree with my friend, the Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett), with respect to the issue of whether it should be "shall" or ''may" in Clause 28. I agree with her that it should be completely scrapped.
On another point, however, I have perhaps a slight disagreement with that Hon. Member, that is, on the appointment of directors to the board. I am not quite as trusting of the Government as she is. She gave the example that SIPRI, the Stockholm Institute, has its directors appointed by the Government. Obviously, however, the Swedish Governments over the last number of years have proven that they can be trusted a little more than has the Government of Canada. I would hate to think, for instance, Mr. Speaker, that someone like Jack Horner, an old Liberal-Tory hack, might be appointed to be chairman of the board of this peace research institute. I would like to see some kind of control on the appointment of directors.
A suggestion was made yesterday by a couple of Hon. Members of the Conservative Party that we might have the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence make these appointments. That is one suggestion I would certainly consider. Another suggestion one might consider is that the standing committee have the power to approve appointments which are initially made by the Governor in Council. We could also turn it around the other way and have the standing committee make one, two, three recommendations to the Governor in Council, who would then choose however many are needed out of those recommended persons. This would have the added benefit of strengthening committees, something which is desirable to most Hon. Members of this House.

Whatever route we choose, whether it be these suggestions or something completely different, I believe we have to change the way in which directors are appointed to the board of this organization. I will give credit-which is something I do not often do-to the Conservative Party. The Hon. Member for Don Vally West said yesterday in this House that this Party would not want this power were it to form the Government. I really hope that if it does form the Government some time in the near or distant future it will really live up to that assertion.
I would like to give an example, Mr. Speaker, of what I have discovered in the last few days as to how the Liberal Government of Canada has skewered this whole peace issue for its own political benefit, and it is something which makes me worry about what it has in mind for the new peace research institute. Just recently I learned about a "new kid on the block" peace group in this country. It is an organization known as INPAX. Very few people have heard of it until very recently. After quite a bit of research I discovered that it is being organized by some young students at the two main universities here in the City of Ottawa. Somehow or other they seem to have gained a lot of influence with Members on the government benches. This is a brand new group. Its main raison d'etre, or current purpose, is to set up a jamboree here in Ottawa at the beginning of September, bringing some 600 students together from various parts of the world to talk about issues of peace. That is a very admirable initiative.
However, my concern is that this group somehow or other has managed to convince the Government-I will say that the final decision has not been made yet but it looks as if it may well be-to give this group $600,000 toward this jamboree which is coming up. I said that this is an admirable initiative. However, given the fact that very little money is available from the Government of Canada to fund national broad based peace groups, why does the Government give something to a brand new group which is centred solely in the City of Ottawa?
There are a lot of questions which have to be answered, Mr. Speaker. One question to which I would like an answer is, why did the federal Government pay for a reception which was held on the Hill here last week, on the invitation of people from this IN PAX group, organized by the office of the Minister for External Relations (Mr. Pepin), with free bar and hot food, which was billed to his office? Organizational details for this reception were handled by the office of the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae). I have a terrible suspicion, Mr. Speaker, that this INPAX group, with its admirable initiative, is really a Liberal front. Somehow the Liberals are trying to get on the peace bandwagon. I would say that if the Government were really interested in educating Canadians about issues of disarmament and peace, there are far better ways to spend $600,000 than on this particular effort.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to caution Hon. Members of this House on both sides that this institute must not be politicized. I was a little disturbed to read first in the press and then in yesterday's Hansard that the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead has decreed or decided that this Bill is fatally

I would hate to think that those Hon. Members are going to kill it. Perhaps it is an indication that they do not want to let this legislation go through. subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in joining in this debate on Bill C-32, which I feel is perhaps one of the most important debates that will come before this session of Parliament, I thought it might be fitting if I first quoted from a person who has had much to do with the nuclear threat which we now live with. I refer, of course, to Albert Einstein who said: "Peace cannot be kept by force. It can only be achieved by understanding."
I think that is a very relevant quote when we are considering something such as is contemplated by Bill C-32, the establishment of what is often referred to as a peace institute. I say that because on the issue of peace I suggest there has never been any dispute over the need for a bipartisan foreign policy or position. In fact, it was the Leader of my Party, the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Mulroney), the Hon. Member for Central Nova, who called for the matters now being generally discussed by us today to be brought before the House for unanimous resolution. I suggest that resolutions agreed to in the House by all Parties of the House have much more moral force than a resolution decided upon by only one man. We in the Official Opposition believe fervently in the need to search constantly for any means to make our country more secure and the world more peaceful.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that in this nuclear age peace is indeed a moral imperative. Yet there is a new dilemma. While the goal of peace is a mark of civilization, we find the democracies which desire peace also live with the fact that if

April 18, 1984
International Peace and Security
they divorce their desire for peace from a commitment to defend freedom, they could easily turn the question of peace into a weapon of blackmail in the hands of the most ruthless. If, in our anxiety to avoid nuclear war, we become consumed with hysteria, nuclear blackmail may well be encouraged. This balancing of power with peace will be the genius of this age. That is our great challenge. Our objective must be to preserve our freedom, our way of life, our civilization and peace. To develop a strategy that relates the end to the means, to build military forces that avoid the choice between an Armageddon and surrender, is a pre-eminent moral, as well as political, problem for our period.
The principle of trying to be better informed by having basic research done with Canadian persons on matters of peace, disarmament and security should be unquestioned, and I dare to say is unquestioned by every Member of this House. It is especially in this context that I feel that the Throne Speech put it quite correctly when it stated that the Government hopes to improve "the climate among nations" and in improving that climate it hopes to acquire knowledge, creativity and a determination to find solutions.
The Throne Speech reflected on Canada's concern about current international tensions. It said that the Government will "create a publicly funded centre to gather, collate and digest the enormous volume of information now available on defence and arms control issues". "Fresh ideas and new proposals, regardless of source, will be studied and promoted", the Throne Speech said. No one has objections to this. However, the draft Bill, Bill C-32, that we are being asked to accept quickly I suggest is little more than a first draft and certainly not even a good first draft of those high hopes that were set out in the Throne Speech at the beginning of this session.
I say that because I think we must not lose sight of the fact that there are two distinct roles that an institute, such as the one whose creation we are debating today, could fill. First, it could be an inward-looking kind of institute, perhaps along the lines of the American National Security Council, funded by the U.S. Government, as we know, which in turn is responsive to government and essentially deals only with the federal Government. Such an inward type of group would fill the role of essentially pooling brain power within the country in this field in order to give the federal Government a very serious input on the matters of the day and as a possible counterbalance to what government may be told by the military, for instance.
The idea is to give government insight and advice in an inhouse advisory group. Such an institute would be useful for a government not only in policy deliberations but also for choosing what arguments could be advanced during negotiations at arms reduction talks. In short, this would be a pooling of brain power and knowledge for the advice of the government of the day, to make it better able to deal with these broad questions of how to secure peace on the one hand while maintaining
proper security. There would be a minimum public exposure with respect to that type of activity.
However, there is an alternative type of activity that an institute could serve. I would suggest, though, that it is an activity in which it must be an entirely independent body in order to perform effectively. It would be an outward-going type of institute that would do original research and would assemble and distribute information. It would possibly advise the government but in no way would be looked upon as speaking for the government. It could advise various groups in society. In short, it would be the type of group that was recently set up in Canada, the Canadian Centre for Arms Control and Disarmament. That is an outward-looking type of group, which I will come back to in a moment.
This is where the Government's dilemma apparently First began. Given what it said in the Throne Speech, we understand that it was unaware that a group had, at that time, been formed in Ottawa. It was called the Canadian Centre for Arms Control and Disarmament. When the Throne Speech referred to a centre, this meant that the word "centre" could not be used in the Bill now before us. That is why we have the word "institute". Again, the Government changed its wording from the Throne Speech to what we have now, a Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security.
I say this because I and I believe most Members in the House were quite startled yesterday to see how prickly the Government, particularly the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), seemed to react with respect to any debate about Bill C-32. You will recall that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) commenced his remarks yesterday at 11.17 a.m. and stated, as reported at page 3118 of Hansard:
In a spirit of consensus and co-operation among all Parties, we remain open to suggestions for further changes to the Bill.
He mentioned that it was, in truth, an independent institute. Yet what did we find within 30 minutes, at 11.42 a.m. yesterday morning, when my colleague, the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) stated at page 3121 of Hansard:
This institute has to be done right the first time.
It triggered the Prime Minister to heckle and intervene through a considerable part of my colleague's speech. The Prime Minister ended up by stating at page 3122:
Don't tell us about the ladies in Halifax.
And:
They do not want you to talk out the institute, which is what you are trying to do.
Within the first 25 minutes of comment on this Bill by the Official Opposition, after having taken the Secretary of State for External Affairs seriously, our first speaker, who in this case was a former Prime Minister, was told by the Prime Minister that he was trying to talk out the Bill.
In debating the Bill before us, we must remember that that type of confrontation did not have to occur. There is no need for it. I can only ask, is that really the tone of a peacemaker? Bear in mind that what we are discussing and what we have
April 18, 1984

heard from the speeches today is general agreement with the principle. All parties have indicated that the idea is worth considering.
We must also accept that this is not a new or unique thought. I read recently that in 1793 the Americans were actively debating what we are debating today. They wanted to set up a peace academy The argument was that if they were to have a department of war, should they not have a department of peace? Oddly enough, that debate with respect to the establishment of a peace academy is now before the Congress of the United States.
The arguments that are being raised there are not dissimilar to the arguments that we have already heard with respect to the Prime Minister's Bill that is now before us. I am saying that I hope all Members in this debate will perhaps accept that it is not the principle that is being debated; it is simply the question of whether the Bill reflects an institution that in truth would serve our goal in a meaningful way.
I have indicated that there are two types of institutions. There is an inward-looking institution that would solely advise the Government, or a more publicly oriented one that would in no way be dependent on the Government. Unfortunately, what we have before us is a hybrid. It is a cross.
I think the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Blais) demonstrated the dilemma that the Government is already living with in his response to an earlier question that I put to him. When I asked him what access the new institute will have to classified information, he said that, of course, he would have to look at each case. When I asked him if he will consult with his allies, bearing in mind that there may be foreign directors on the board of this institute, he said that he would, of course, have to take it up with his NATO allies.
If this institute was solely confined to advising government, that would not be necessary. It would be a think-tank solely to advise the Government. However, because of the public aspect and that it is a hybrid, it will do one of two things. It will either make classified information available and possibly run the risk of having leaks, or it will withhold all information. If it withholds all information, the institute will not be able to function fully. Much of the information which it should have at its disposal will be denied, for the simple reason that those who are furnishing the information will say: "We are uneasy about into whose hands the information will ultimately fall". That is the dilemma in which this early draft of a Bill has left us. It is why during my remarks this afternoon I want to point out the tragedy of the ongoing dialogue that was taking place between all three Parties, the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) and the Leader of the Socialist Party (Mr. Broadbent) being broken off. Why? Why on the twelfth of this month was the ongoing discussion as to how to make this institution truly independent, how to ensure it will not needlessly affect and impact on the 26-odd organizations that are already in this field in Canada broken off? Why were those discussions terminated? Why was the Official Opposition and presumably the Socialist Party told: "In any event we are introducing the Bill, and we can discuss it later"?
International Peace and Security
You know that the type of thing that was being raised at that time, Mr. Speaker, was the question, for example, of the appointment of the board of directors for this institute. It was suggested that before any board is settled there should be a consensus of this Parliament. The chairman, the executive director, and the 15 other directors could be suggested name-wise by the various parties. We should arrive at a consensus. But what we heard in reply was "That is our business". There is to this date no indication who the chairman might be, who the executive director might be, or indeed who any of the directors might be. All that we were assured of is that we would be given the right to nominate but without even a suggestion that a nominee would be appointed.
I believe if you read Clause 3 of the Bill you will see the importance to which I am referring, Mr. Speaker. What we are establishing in this Bill is this, and I quote directly:
3. A corporation is hereby established to be called the Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security consisting of a Board of Directors that is composed of a Chairman, an Executive Director and not more than 15 other directors to be appointed as provided in sections 6 to 8.
The latter in effect says "to be appointed by the Government".
What we are creating here is essentially an institution that has to be constituted by a board of directors. They will speak for this institute. I suggest it is absolutely irresponsible on an issue such as peace and security for us in Parliament to pass a Bill like this in its present form and leave up to the government of the day the right to say who in fact will comprise the institute.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Let me touch, if I may, on the other important questions. For example, we have already touched on-certainly my colleague the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) has-the right of government to require the institute to come up with certain studies. I think there is general agreement that the word "shall" must get watered down to something more like "may". But again there is the question of the reporting by this institute. There is no guarantee in the present Bill that the reports of the institute will go uncensored, or that the institute will be free to publish as it sees fit with or without qualification.
For example, the Canadian Centre for Arms Control and Disarmament has just brought out its first edition of the Arms Control Chronicle. I recommend that all Members read it. It consists of 14 pages. It is a very interesting overview of the past month in this field. I would hate on the one hand to have any suggestion that this entity be killed off by this new institute we are now discussing. Second, I would hope the freedom this centre has to publish what is in its chronicle this month would be the type of freedom without government interference that the new institute contemplated in Bill C-32 would have if it is formed.
In conclusion-

Mr. Speaker, now they are all going to leave! The basic thrust of my speech can be stated very directly. The nuclear threat, East-West relations, international peace and security, defence, arms control and disarmament are so important to all of our constituents, including my three young children, that the institute proposed in Bill C-32 must not be tainted from birth as a partisan, dependent body.
The burden of my argument here is that, as currently drafted, the Bill is a prescription for an institute very susceptible to following the wishes of any government in office. Why do I say that? First, the language of the Bill establishes the institute as neither independent from government nor part of government. We on this side would prefer language which clearly protects the institute from interference by a government, and, conversely, if you like, an elected government from the institute. What we have here is neither fish nor fowl, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps it is some form of a stew.
Second, the funding issue is crucial to the independence question. The present position of the Government is, I gather, that the Department of National Defence and the Department of External Affairs will contribute jointly to the institute on an annual basis by government appropriations. However, this model, Sir, keeps the institute on a very short leash. Would its independence not be likely to suffer accordingly? The Damocles sword would be that if the institute displeased a government in year one, its funding would be cut, or substantially altered, in year two.
I remind Hon. Members that only yesterday in British Columbia, the Government of Premier Bennett cut funding to a women's group action committee, and I fear the same thing might happen to this very important institute. Surely, Mr. Speaker, a more responsible approach from the standpoint of independence and non-partisanship would be the endowment route. We should establish an endowment fund and allow the institute to operate from endowment resources.

Third, the proposed formula for setting up the Institute raises the serious question of the Institute's total independence vis-a-vis the Government. The Chairman shall be appointed by the Governor in Council for a term not exceeding three years. The Executive Director shall be appointed by the Governor in Council to hold office for a term not exceeding five years. Fifteen directors shall be appointed by the Governor in Council to hold office for respective mandates not exceeding three years.
Who will they be? I maintain that, considering our experience with many federal agencies, the Canadian directors will be defeated Liberal candidates, presidents of Liberal riding associations and other individuals known for their partisan activities.
Why not a more imaginative appointment structure to ensure more independent-minded and competent people on the board, Sir? For example, a phrase in Clauses 6, 7 or 8 indicating that any person appointed might have before appointment "eminence in peace, security or disarmament matters"? Or a phrase such as "appointed after a consensus" by all members of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence? Why not a phrase indicating that nominees must have the approval of the Opposition Leaders?
April 18, 1984

It is hardly reassuring to hear the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) say here yesterday that the Government will seek nominations from opposition Parties before making appointments. From too much past experience we know this Government will wait only long enough to hear our proposals and then go ahead and appoint its own choices. The Minister said yesterday that he wants the institute to be "apolitical and non-partisan". We agree. Why not then build in an appointment mechanism which guarantees these qualities for our institute? Why not some phrase indicating that the chairman should be appointed by the Governor in Council "upon recommendation by the board of directors"? Similarly, why not have the executive director appointed by Governor in Council "upon the recommendation of the board of directors"? All of these suggestions would enhance the independence and credibility of the institute.
If we want truly independent-minded directors of the institute, it would also seem to me that Clause 21 should make it clear that members of the Public Service of Canada are not eligible to become directors. Can a public servant, albeit competent and respected, be truly independent? The current wording appears to make them eligible. On the other hand, why not allow the institute to second public servants for "a period of up to three years" as staff members? Clause 12 should be changed to reflect this.

In the course of this debate, there has been considerable emphasis on the implications of Clause 28 which provides that, at the request of the Minister, the Institute "shall provide" in relation to any issue involving "international peace and security" ... In fact, this clause might allow the Minister to set the order of priority of the Institute's activities. By substituting "may provide" for "shall provide", and "Government" or "Parliament" for "Minister", we might be able to reduce the risk of having such situations occur.

Another error in principle lies in Clause 5(c), which appears to authorize the institute to publish studies and reports in the name of the institute. Basic intellectual integrity requires that institutional research be published on an attributable basis. That clause should be changed to include the phrase "on an attribution basis".
Let us look for a moment at three other similar federal agencies in this regard. First, the Science Council of Canada, which provides independent policy advice to the Government, works only with publicly available information, makes no grants and has no research capability. In my judgment the credibility of the Science Council suffered when those opposite filled the chairmanship with a retiring Liberal politician in the Province of Ontario. Stuart Smith is to be sure an intelligent individual, but in my judgment the Government tainted the work of the Science Council with his appointment because it indicated to one and all that it preferred an active Liberal to some eminent, non-partisan scientist as chairman. How do we
International Peace and Security know it will not do the same with this institute unless we build in legislative guarantees for its integrity from the start?
Second, Mr. Speaker, the International Development Research Centre, and I will refer to it as IDRC, shares similarities in its organizational structure with the institute, including the provision for foreign directors. In passing, I wonder why we need foreign directors. Do we not have enough qualified men and women across this talented country with sufficient eminence in the field to fill all the directorships in this institution with distinction? I think so. However, let us look at only some of the Canadian directors of the IDRC as an indication of whether the present Government really intends to make non-partisan and apolitical appointments when given the chance.
The first name on my list is Donald S. Macdonald, chairman of the board of the IDRC. He is a former Liberal MP now earning $800 per day as a Royal Commissioner who produced an interim report two days ago which won something less than wide critical acclaim. Second is Maurice LaClair, CN President and a former medical doctor who did a stint in the Prime Minister's Office. Third is Ivan Head, president and chief executive officer, and formerly an adviser to the Prime Minister. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, will Tom Axworthy, Frank Fowler and other members of the Prime Minister's Office be the most likely candidates for early nomination since all of them will, I assume, be technically out of work as of June 16? Fourth, Mr. Speaker, we have John Stewart, formerly a Liberal MP and recently appointed a Liberal senator.
I do not know enough about the other Canadian directors to be certain, but from past experience I doubt if many of them are politically neutral. However, my point is that unless we build in non-partisanship in this Bill, the strong probability is that a dying Government will see that the institute is politically tainted from the start. In the case of the IDRC, there is at least some attempt in Section 10 to assure excellence in governors by specifying that "at least 11 of the governors must have experience in the field of international development". Unfortunately, this good intention is largely vitiated by the rest of the section which says "or experience or training in the natural or social sciences or technology". That is a pretty big basket and it includes an awful lot of people.
The third body is the Law Reform Commission of Canada which, since its founding in 1971, to my knowledge has never actively criticized the Government of Canada or its policy. I am told that nothing in the legislation founding the Commission deals with this question, so again we must look to the partisanship or non-partisanship of members of that Commission. Let us start with the first chairman, Mr. Justice Patrick Hartt. I have no knowledge of his political affiliation and I say nothing further on that. However, the second chairman was Mr. Justice Antonio Lamer, past president of the Young Liberals of Quebec, I am informed. The Third chairman was Mr. Justice Frank Muldoon, who as you probably know, Mr. Speaker, is a past Liberal candidate provincially in Manitoba. The present chairman is Mr. Justice Allan Linden. In fairness,
